lines.text:
The Magic of the Stage — A Visit to the Theatre

Last Friday, Class 8B went on a school trip to the Grand Theatre to watch a performance of 'A Midsummer Night's Dream.' It was the first time many students had been inside a real theatre.

The building was impressive. The lobby had high ceilings and old posters on the walls. Students collected their tickets at the box office and left their coats in the cloakroom. An usher handed each student a programme with information about the play and the actors.

Inside, the auditorium was much bigger than expected. The orchestra seats were on the ground floor, close to the stage. Above, the balcony offered a wider view. A few box seats — small private areas on the side — had red velvet chairs. The students sat in Row G, near the middle, with a clear view of the proscenium — the frame around the stage opening.

Before the play started, the curtain was closed. When the lights went down and the curtain rose, the audience saw a beautiful backdrop painted to look like a forest. Spotlights lit the centre of the stage. Actors entered from the wings — the hidden areas on each side. The apron — the part of the stage closest to the audience — was where most of the dialogue happened.

The costumes were wonderful. The fairy queen wore a long robe, a crown, and a cape. The actors' stage makeup and face paint made their expressions visible even from the balcony. A mirror backstage helped each actor check their appearance before going on stage.

Props brought the story to life. A throne stood in the centre for the royal scenes. A goblet sat on the table. Candles and lanterns created a magical atmosphere. A treasure chest appeared through a trapdoor in the floor. A banner and flags decorated the stage for the final celebration.

Behind the scenes, many people worked hard. The director guided the actors. The stage manager organised everything backstage. A lighting designer controlled the spotlights and the fly system that raised and lowered scenery. A sound technician managed the music and sound effects. A costume designer created every outfit. A set builder constructed the backdrop and the scenery. A prompter sat near the stage, ready to help any actor who forgot their lines.

The performance lasted two hours. At the end, the actors bowed, and the audience clapped and cheered. Walking back through the lobby, one student said, 'I want to be an actor.' Another said, 'I want to design the costumes.' The theatre had done its job — it had brought a story to life and inspired everyone who watched.

lines.text: British spelling: 'theatre'. American spelling: 'theater'. Both are correct. Similarly: British 'programme' / American 'program'. The West End (London) and Broadway (New York) are the world's two most famous theatre districts.

lines.text: William Shakespeare (1564–1616) is considered the greatest English-language playwright. His plays — Hamlet, Romeo and Juliet, Macbeth, A Midsummer Night's Dream — are still performed worldwide. Many English idioms come from Shakespeare.

lines.text: London's West End is home to famous theatres like the Old Vic, the National Theatre, and the Lyceum. Long-running shows include The Phantom of the Opera, Les Misérables, and The Lion King. 'West End show' implies a top-quality production.

lines.text: A 'pantomime' or 'panto' is a uniquely British tradition — a comedic theatrical performance at Christmas, usually based on fairy tales. The audience shouts 'He's behind you!' and 'Oh no it isn't!' It's a family event, not a mime show.

lines.text: British theatre etiquette: arrive on time, turn off your phone, don't talk during the performance, don't eat noisy food, and applaud at the end. Late arrivals may not be seated until the interval.

lines.text: Two errors: (1) 'Good at + noun/-ing': 'good at acting', 'good at maths.' Never 'good in.' (2) 'Become + a/an + job title': 'become an actress', 'become a director.' The article is required.

lines.text: 'Last' (meaning 'continue for a period') is an intransitive verb — it does not take a passive form. 'The show lasted three hours.' 'The performance lasted until midnight.' Never 'was lasted' — it's already active.

lines.text: 'Twice' is the standard word for 'two times.' 'Once' = one time. 'Twice' = two times. 'Three times', 'four times', etc. are fine. But 'two times' sounds unnatural in most contexts — use 'twice.'
